# 2009 CS Q12: Language generated by S -> aSa | bSb | a | b

## Question

$S \to aSa \mid bSb \mid a \mid b$

The language generated by the above grammar over the alphabet $\lbrace a, b \rbrace$ is the set of

- (A) all palindromes.
- (B) all odd length palindromes.
- (C) strings that begin and end with the same symbol.
- (D) all even length palindromes.

<details class="success" markdown="1">
<summary>Answer</summary>

**B**

</details>

<details class="info" markdown="1">
<summary>Solution</summary>

Every derivation ends by replacing $S$ with a single $a$ or $b$. Each earlier step wraps the string in a matching pair, $aSa$ or $bSb$. Example:

$$S \Rightarrow aSa \Rightarrow abSba \Rightarrow ababa.$$

So the language is a single centre symbol with matching pairs added around it: **all palindromes of odd length**: (B).

- (A) is false: the grammar never gives an even-length string, so $aa$ and $abba$ are palindromes it cannot derive.
- (C) is false: $aa$ begins and ends with $a$, but it is not generated. Neither is $abaa$.
- (D) is false: no even-length string is generated at all.

**Code check:** all strings the grammar derives up to length $11$ were generated by program: $126$ strings, exactly equal to the set of odd-length palindromes of length $\le 11$ over $\lbrace a, b \rbrace$. No even-length string appeared.

**Key idea:** a rule that wraps $S$ in a matching pair plus a single-symbol base case generates odd-length palindromes.

</details>
